title: Cascode Current Mirrors
intro: Channel-length modulation spoils a mirror whenever the output device's $V_{DS}$ differs from the reference device's. Either make $V_{DS2}$ follow $V_{DS1}$ (the cascode mirror) or make $V_{DS1}$ follow $V_{DS2}$ (resistor and low-voltage cascode schemes).

blocks.text: First approach: cascode the output

A cascode device M3 on top of M2 shields M2's drain from the output, so $V_{DS2}$ barely moves. To make it equal to $V_{DS1} = V_{GS1}$, the cascode gate needs $V_b = V_{GS3} + V_{GS1}$. Stacking a second diode-connected device M0 on M1 produces exactly that, provided $V_{GS0} = V_{GS3}$. Then $V_Y = V_X$ and the copy is accurate, even with body effect, because M0 and M3 sit at the same source voltage and see the same body bias.

blocks.alt: Cascode current mirror. Left: IREF from VDD flows into diode-connected M0 stacked on diode-connected M1; node X between them. Right: M3 stacked on M2; node Y between them, output current at the top of M3. M0 and M3 gates are tied (node N), M1 and M2 gates are tied.
blocks.caption: Cascode mirror. Size $W_3/W_0 = W_2/W_1$ with $L_3 = L_0$ so that $V_{GS3} = V_{GS0}$; M0 and M3 are often minimum length, M1 and M2 may be longer.

blocks.text: Headroom cost
With identical devices and no body effect, $V_N = V_{GS0} + V_{GS1}$, and M3 stays saturated while the output is above $V_N - V_{TH}$:

A cascode current source could work down to $2V_{ov}$ if $V_b$ were only $V_{GS3} + V_{ov2}$, but then $V_{DS2}$ would be one overdrive while $V_{DS1} = V_{GS1}$, and the copy would be inaccurate. The plain cascode mirror wastes one $V_{TH}$ of headroom because $V_{DS2} = V_{GS2}$ when $V_{GS2} - V_{TH}$ would do.
Large-signal behaviour as the output falls

Above $V_N - V_{TH}$ both output devices are saturated and $I_{out} = I_{REF}$. Below it, M3 enters triode first (M2 cannot leave saturation first, because that would need M3's current to fall while its $V_{GS}$ rises). M3 then needs more gate-source voltage, so node Y drops, M2's current sags slightly, and the output resistance collapses because M3's $g_m$ shrinks in triode. Once Y falls below $V_{GS2} - V_{TH}$, M2 enters triode and the current drops steeply to zero at $V_{out} = 0$.

Second approach: lower the reference device's VDS

Instead, bring $V_{DS1}$ down to about one overdrive. A resistor $R_1$ between M1's drain and gate with $R_1 I_{REF} \approx V_{TH1}$ gives $V_{DS1} = V_{GS1} - R_1 I_{REF} \approx V_{GS1} - V_{TH1}$, and a cascode bias $V_b = V_{GS3} + (V_{GS1} - V_{TH1})$ puts $V_{DS2}$ at the same value. items: Weakness 1: $R_1 I_{REF}$ and $V_{TH}$ drift differently with process and temperature, so the condition $R_1 I_{REF} \approx V_{TH1}$ is not robust.

Weakness 2: generating $V_b = V_{GS3} + (V_{GS1} - V_{TH1})$ is awkward. A diode M5 plus a resistor $R_6$ ($V_b = V_{GS5} + R_6 I_6$) needs an IR drop to track $V_{GS}$, which it does not. Using a diode M5 for $V_{GS}$ and a copy of the M1-$R_1$ pair (M6 with $R_6$, $I_6 = I_{REF}$, $R_6 = R_1$, $(W/L)_6 = (W/L)_1$) for the overdrive makes the terms track, apart from small body-effect differences.

blocks.text: The low-voltage cascode

A cleaner way to make $V_{DS1}$ equal $V_{DS2}$ is to stack the reference devices as a cascode and take M1's gate from the top of the stack. The cascode gate $V_b$ is shared with M3, so $V_{DS1} = V_b - V_{GS0}$ and, with $V_{GS0} = V_{GS3}$, $V_{DS1} = V_{DS2}$ automatically. This low-voltage (or wide-swing) cascode is used more widely than the plain cascode mirror.

blocks.alt: Low-voltage cascode mirror. Left: IREF flows into the drain of M0 (node X), stacked on M1 (node A between them); a wire from X goes to the gates of M1 and M2, hopping over the Vb line. M0 and M3 gates are tied to an external bias Vb. Right: M3 stacked on M2 with node B between them and the output at the top of M3.
blocks.caption: Low-voltage cascode mirror: $V_A = V_B = V_b - V_{GS0}$, so both bottom devices see the same $V_{DS}$ of about one overdrive.

blocks.text: Both reference devices must be saturated: M0 needs $V_b - V_{TH0} \le V_X = V_{GS1}$, and M1 needs $V_{GS1} - V_{TH1} \le V_A = V_b - V_{GS0}$. Hence

A solution exists only if $V_{GS0} - V_{TH0} < V_{TH1}$, so M0 is sized for an overdrive well below a threshold. For the least headroom, $V_b$ sits at (or slightly above) the lower bound, and the output works down to about $2V_{ov}$. $V_b$ can be produced by a diode-connected device (supplying $V_{GS}$) on top of a device biased to drop one overdrive, or by a diode plus a resistor, which is less well controlled.
Variations
Replica biasing when there is no room for a cascode

If the tail of a differential pair has too little headroom for a cascode, make $V_{DS1}$ copy the tail's $V_{DS}$ instead. Put a scaled replica of the pair, with the same lengths and widths in the ratio $W_r/W_d = I_{REF}/I_{SS}$, on top of the reference device and drive its gates from the same inputs. Its source node then tracks the tail node P even when the input CM level moves (until the replica enters triode).
A regulated mirror

Another high-impedance output uses feedback rather than stacking: a transistor M3 senses the output node X and pulls on the gate node N of the output device M1, via the diode device M2. If $V_X$ rises by $\Delta V$, M1's current tends to rise by $\Delta V/r_{o1}$, but M3 draws $g_{m3}\Delta V$ from N, lowering $V_N$ by about $g_{m3}\Delta V/g_{m2}$ and cutting M1's current by $g_{m1}g_{m3}\Delta V/g_{m2}$. Choosing $g_{m1}g_{m3}/g_{m2} \approx 1/r_{o1}$ cancels the change. The output must stay above $V_{TH3}$ for M3 to regulate, which is more than the $V_{DS,sat}$ a cascode would need, and at very high $V_X$ M3 absorbs all of $I_{REF}$ and turns M1 off.

In nanometer processes $\lambda$ is so large that even a cascode mirror's output current still varies visibly with $V_{out}$ across its whole saturated range; check mirror accuracy in simulation over the real output range.

blocks.title: Headroom of the two cascode mirrors
blocks.text: All devices have $V_{TH} = 0.4\text{ V}$ and $V_{ov} = 0.2\text{ V}$. What is the minimum output voltage of a plain cascode mirror and of a low-voltage cascode mirror?
solution: Low-voltage: about $2V_{ov} = 0.4\text{ V}$, half as much.

blocks.title: Choosing the low-voltage cascode bias
blocks.text: In a low-voltage cascode, $V_{TH} = 0.4\text{ V}$ for all devices, M0 runs at $V_{ov0} = 0.15\text{ V}$ and M1 at $V_{ov1} = 0.2\text{ V}$. Find the allowed range of $V_b$ and a good choice.
solution: Lower bound: $V_{GS0} + V_{ov1} = 0.75\text{ V}$. Upper bound: $V_{GS1} + V_{TH0} = 1.0\text{ V}$.
Choose slightly above the lower bound, around 0.8 V, to keep the output headroom near $2V_{ov}$ with some margin.
blocks.answer: $0.75\text{ V} \le V_b \le 1.0\text{ V}$; pick about 0.8 V.

blocks.title: Largest reference current
blocks.text: A cascode mirror runs from 1.8 V; the reference source needs 0.3 V. Both $V_{TH} = 0.4\text{ V}$, $\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_0 = 4\text{ mA/V}^2$ and $\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_1 = 2\text{ mA/V}^2$. Find $I_{REF,max}$.
solution: Require $V_{GS0} + V_{GS1} \le 1.8 - 0.3 = 1.5\text{ V}$, so the two overdrives must sum to $1.5 - 0.8 = 0.7\text{ V}$.

blocks.title: Is the resistor-shifted device still a diode?
blocks.text: M1 has $g_m = 1\text{ mS}$ and $r_o = 20\text{ k}\Omega$, with $R_1 = 4\text{ k}\Omega$ between drain and gate. Find the small-signal impedance at its drain.
solution: $\frac{R_1 + r_o}{1 + g_m r_o} = \frac{24\text{ k}\Omega}{21} = 1.14\text{ k}\Omega$, close to $1/g_m = 1\text{ k}\Omega$.
